chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from more than one, from Aban, from Ibn Abi Ya'fur, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

If they differ regarding the pledge, and one says 'I pledged it for a thousand [dinars]' and the other says 'for a hundred dirhams', he says: 'The owner of the thousand is asked for proof; if he has no proof, the owner of the hundred swears an oath.'

And if the pledge is less than what was pledged or more, or they differ, and one says 'It is a pledge' and the other says 'It is a deposit', he says: 'The proof is upon the owner of the deposit; if he has no proof, the owner of the pledge swears an oath.'

key_terms.صَاحِبُ اَلْأَلْفِ: The owner of the thousand (claiming higher value)

ai.seo_question: How does Shia jurisprudence resolve disputes over the value or type of a pledged item?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the principle of *al-bayyinah 'ala al-mudda'i* (proof is upon the claimant) in financial disputes, specifically addressing discrepancies in pledged value or classification between *rahn* (pledge) and *wadi'ah* (deposit). It demonstrates the Shia jurisprudential application of evidentiary standards where the burden of proof rests on the party asserting a higher value or a specific legal status, with an oath serving as the fallback mechanism to resolve uncertainty. This ruling underscores the importance of clear documentation and witness testimony in Islamic commercial law to prevent unjust enrichment.
